utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you're to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Mr. Katic, yesterday we started your examination. At the moment, when we finished yesterday, you were talking about the position of Grbavica. However, tell me one more thing: You mentioned high-rise buildings. These high-rise buildings, if you compare them, which ones were dominant there in that area. I don't want to lead you in any way.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The high-rises on the other side of the Miljacka river, in relation to the high-rise buildings on Grbavica, they're higher, especially the high-rise building in the street of Bratstvo-Jedinstvo. That's what it was called then, on the other side of the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of these high-rise buildings have their own names, something like that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did. How should I put this? There were the Unis buildings, Unis sky-scrapers at Marindvor. They are much higher. Then there was the Assembly building, which is also taller than the buildings on the Miljacka. And now I cannot remember exactly. Now, what do we call this? This building with a lot of balconies by the Bridge of Brotherhood and Unity, "Bratstvo I Jedinstvo." I cannot remember exactly now. I cannot remember its exact name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we deal with another problem now. Grbavica is where it is, as you explained. What is referred to is the existence of a blockade of Sarajevo. Can you say something about that? As far as your very own feeling there, you were there, at Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot understand at all, or rather, I cannot say that we had blockaded Sarajevo, or rather, this feeling of a blockade. As I look at Grbavica itself, I think that at Grbavica, I was in a three quarters blockade, if I can put it that way. Blocked from three sides practically. There were these geographic positions, as I already said: On one side Debelo Brdo; on the other side, Mojmilo; and on the third side, high-rise buildings and also the hill of Zuc behind Pofalici. Also, when I look at the municipality of Novo Sarajevo and from Grbavica, the other part of Novo Sarajevo municipality, you could only go along one street, Zagrebacka Street, which went from Grbavica to Vraca to Bijelo Poljska street then to Lukavica. And Lukavica was exposed to fire, infantry fire, from the Mojmilo hill and also parts of Dobrinja, 1 and 4, or rather, that part of the neighbourhood of Dobrinja where the separation line was; although, geographically speaking, this did not belong to the municipality of Novo Sarajevo then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to show you a document, which I got from the Prosecution, and that the Prosecution will use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand the witness's evidence. Your evidence, then, is that it is not only the Muslims, the ABiH, who were blocked in, that the Serbs were also blocked in, at least in some areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Your Honour. I am just talking about parts of the municipality of Serb New Sarajevo, and that is Grbavica, as I said yesterday. As for the rest of the city of Sarajevo, geographically speaking, it was in it like a kidney in a body. And from the point of view of the altitude involved, the population was exposed to attacks. And if I can put it this way, we just had this narrow passageway, down Zagrebacka Street, from Grbavica via Vraca to Lukavica, and further on the territory of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm still trying to understand the Defence case. Would it be correct to say that your case, then, is that the whole situation in Sarajevo, including the history, the background, the geographical positions of the various forces, was completely different from that which was outlined in the Prosecution's case, and, in fact, makes implausible the Prosecution case and, therefore, less credible the allegations made of terror and of the crimes with which the accused has been charged? You are presenting to the Chamber a completely different picture, which renders implausible the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honour, Mr. President, Judge Robinson, of course, although, I was in a position here several times to make my final arguments; nevertheless, I think that this is something that I shall specify at the end of the proceedings. Now, through this witness, I'm trying to ascertain what the factual situation was in different parts of Sarajevo. At this moment, what we are discussing is Grbavica, but we are going to call other witnesses and we are going to prove precisely that, through the case of individual municipalities; that is to say, that the dominant points in Sarajevo were in the hands of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the Serb positions were always at the foot of these hills, and that it was very difficult to have a proper separation, especially Grbavica, Hrasno, Nedzarici, Ilidza. Ilidza is a spot that is part of town. So all these areas, in our belief and in terms of the case we want to prove, were so intertwined, that if we look at the Prosecution case as charged in the indictment, that cannot be proven at all. So this is what we intend to show through our own case. That situations were quite different from those referred to in the indictment. This witness is just speaking about one very important segment of these positions, the Serb positions that were within the heart of the city; that is to say, in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. When I say in the heart of the city, it was mixed. One river-bank was in the hands of one army and the other side of the Miljacka was in the hands of the other army. No one was in a blockade there. This was an urban clash, a war conflict in the heart of a city, the dominant features in this area in 80 percent of all the cases involved. I categorically state that it has already been proven through the evidence that we have heard. In my view and in the view of the Defence, it was quite obvious who was on these hills in -- it is my belief and my conviction that as we heard the Prosecution case, we did see who held Mojmilo, Debelo Brdo, Stup Brdo, Zuc, Grdonj, not to mention all the hills now. Of course, there are other areas now that are yet to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, as for the blockade, now when I show you a document, the 65 ter number is 03179. This is a Prosecution document. It is a newspaper article from 1994. I would just like to draw your attention to two paragraphs in order to explain what this blockade looked like. Please, in addition to this physical blockade -- yes, see, the text is here. Can you recognise the text? What newspaper is this? It says at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srpska Vojska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there an English translation for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a Prosecution exhibit that was tendered after the witness took the solemn declaration. I don't know if there is a translation. I didn't receive one, but this is a Prosecution document. It is a document that the Prosecutor wants to use. I looked for a translation, but I couldn't find one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this a Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It's on our list, Your Honour, that we have sent over to the Defence. Whether we will actually use it or not, we don't know at this point. Translation is pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But if you wish to use it, then you should she that there is a translation, Mr. Tapuskovic. Well, let us see. You wish to -- yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Ms. Bosnjakovic did a little more checking and has found the English translation. It was just recently done, so can we get just get. One minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, had I had just one day, I would have had this translated, for sure, through a translator that I would have engaged, but I got this only yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe we should move ahead and come back to it. Go ahead and then return to it when the translation is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The translation is there now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, the translation is there now. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, you talked about this blockade a few moments ago, as you saw it from Grbavica. Since we are discussing the blockade now, I would like to draw your attention to the one-but-last paragraph of this text. You told a journalist about something, and what it says here, does that correspond to what you think and what you experienced while you were there? It's the one-but last paragraph. Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sarajevo is under a blockade."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we have page 2 of the translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sarajevo is under a blockade but not of our forces, rather, 'several Muslim armies,'" quote/unquote. "Everyone has his own army and his own quarter. These private companies do not allow anyone to leave the town, and there are so many people who would like to get out, more than 50.000 Serbs for sure. While an HVO unit was in front of us, Serbs used to cross the Miljacka river every day. However, Muslims no longer trust Croatian soldiers. They are controlling them rigorously, so they cannot close their eyes any longer."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that something that was dominant at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While you were president of the municipality, as a president of the municipality, were you able to make a decision sometimes concerning crossings over from one side to the other? Did you undertake any actions in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't do anything or stop people from leaving from Grbavica to the other side. However, on the 21st of March, or rather, on the 24th of March, 1994, with the approval of UNPROFOR and both sides, the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge was opened, enabling citizens from both sides of the river Miljacka to cross over. That was done in cooperation the civilian authorities of both sides, as well as with representatives of UNPROFOR, so to speak, and the police from both sides. This was, in a way, a crossing without any blockades at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order not to go back again to this article concerning the shooting that you mentioned yesterday, can you add some more information about the issue of sniping?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I said that I know what a sniper rifle was, but I didn't see any of them on either side. There was gun-fire from infantry weapons, and I can freely say that Grbavica was an area covered with lots of blankets, sheets, concrete blocks, and other material in order to create passages for civilians across certain streets in Grbavica. As I said, the separation lines were in Grbavica at about 30 metres. Soldiers would come to their trenches and their posts; and in order to do that, they had to protect themselves on the incoming route with various concrete tubes and canvas sheets in order not to be hit from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we still have the document on this screen, I'm going to show you some photographs. But can you please look at paragraph 3 of this article, and if you can read it out loud. Is this consistent with what you were just telling us? Please read it out loud, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It starts: "This is..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That the proper page is not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. May we have the correct page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read it now, because the Judges now can look for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This is the most forward part of the front line of Republika Srpska and the most dangerous one. We are more than happy, but at the same time we feel uncomfortable if the day ends without victims, uncomfortable because something is not right."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The rest is something written by the journalist, and it doesn't have anything to do with your evidence. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us something more about this newspaper, about the publication? What kind of newspaper is this, its orientation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I really don't know what kind of presentation is in this newspaper. I know that I gave statements and interviews. What I said and read here, I stand by it, but I can also say right away that I hadn't read this before or seen this newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I shan't pursue any further on that. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you are right, but I would, nevertheless, insist for the witness to take a look so that we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is written underneath this whole article. There's an indication there. It's the name of the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srpska Vojska. But I didn't receive this newspaper in my office. I didn't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document please be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, yesterday, you talked about you becoming president of the assembly of Novo Sarajevo on the 13th of March, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After that date, until the end of the war, what did your duties involve?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was exclusively involved in civilian duties. Immediately at the very outset of my duties of the president of the municipality and on the basis of the statute, I changed --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you first answer directly my question. What kind of duties did you discharge? Can you just tell me briefly in what kind of duties were you involved from that point until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved exclusively in civilian affairs and nothing other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Speaking about the highest international officials, who were you in contact with at one point in time at the very end?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am exceptionally honoured to say this, but I cannot remember all the high representatives from all over the world. Towards the very end of the war, the premises of the Novo Sarajevo municipality were visited by Mr. Kofi Annan, who was later elected president of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to show you a Prosecution Exhibit, 65 ter 03174. It will take too much -- actually, it won't take too much time to read it because it is a short document. I kindly ask you to read it as fast as possible, and then I will pose just one question to you, or perhaps two questions.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does this have to do with your civilian function? In what capacity did you receive him at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the capacity of the president of Novo Sarajevo municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the problem that arose a few days after -- if you look at this date, at that time? That's 28 of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That goes by five days beyond the framework of the indictment, and I would ask the Trial Chamber, their leave to put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But can you answer it, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not clear to me, 28th November 1995, that's the date; and on the 21st of November, 1995, the Dayton Peace Accords were signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But look at the last -- or the end of the last sentence in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signatures of the three leaders in the Dayton carry certain weight. There were no -- and no changes were envisaged in the agreement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was not referring to this. What was happening with the Serbian population at that time in the territory of your municipality? That was what my question was about.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that each municipality in the Serbian town of Sarajevo was scheduled for the implementation of the Dayton Accord. The Novo Sarajevo municipality, or rather, Grbavica was supposed to have it implemented as part of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 18th of March, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not asking you -- I'm not asking you about political connotations. I'm asking you about how the people, the residents of that municipality, were behaving. What was it that they started doing after that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people were already thinking where to move from Grbavica. Many of them left in January for other parts of Republika Srpska, from Pale, Visegrad, Brcko, Teslic, all the way to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So were those the problems already existing at the time when you met with Kofi Annan?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, these problems did not exist at the time that we discussed them on the 28th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What led to the Serbs leaving Grbavica and the other parts that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there had been a war going on there for four years. There was no love there. People were dying. There was no trust on any side. Serbs went to the territories that in accordance with the Dayton Peace Accord belonged to Republika Srpska; and Muslims, or Bosniaks, and Croats, went to the territory that, again under the Dayton Accords, remained as part of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many Serbs remained in Novo Sarajevo after the war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war, about 10.000 inhabitants remained in the territory of Novo Sarajevo municipality, in the part that, under the Dayton Peace Accords, was part of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And at the time when it was still controlled by the Republika Srpska army, how many of them were there? How many inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, around 25.000 people lived in Novo Sarajevo municipality, in Grbavica, and in other areas that were part of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have to go back to the very beginning. Did you have any duties? Did you hold any posts in the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party, apart from what you have just told us that you were a deputy in the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never held any other posts in the Serbian Democratic Party, except, of course, for being a deputy. I never was a member of the main board of the Serbian Democratic Party. I was not even on the municipal board, and I don't think that I was in the local commune board either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you spoke at length yesterday about how it all began. You said that Pofalici incident happened, Mojmilo incident happened, in May and June respectively. Did it dawn on you at that point what was actually going on? I don't want to lead you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those things that happened, happened. And when I became the president --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's the time-period that I'm yet to question you about. I'm asking you immediately after the Pofalici incident and the Mojmilo incident; that would be the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a problem with the routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that stage, did you become a member of a body, after those conflicts broke out?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. I became a member of the commission of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo as a representative of the deputies of the Serbian Democratic Party, or rather, I represented all the deputies in the municipal assembly. And I have to say that because at that time I was the only person with a university degree, I was nominated as a member of this commission for the Novo Sarajevo municipality, and this commission was set up by Mr. Karadzic, the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now show you a 65 ter document, 03172. Well, you can see -- this document that you have now before you, does this accurately depict the situation, this account that you have just given us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. And as I've already said, this document was signed by the president of the Republic, Mr. Karadzic. He, in fact, nominated the members too. And if I may say so, I saw this document three years ago, I think, when I was interviewed by the investigators of the ICTY. And if I may add, the person under number 1, the republican commissioner, was the Minister, the deputy in the Republika Srpska assembly, Mr. Petko Cancar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me -- I have already put it to that you the incidents at Pofalici and Mojmilo had already happened. Can you please look at the date on this document and the first paragraph of this document. What were the circumstances in which this decision was taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the accused has warned me that the English translation is not identical to the original, and he is right because the date is the 17th of July, and in B/C/S you can see that the date is the 21st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Completely different dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The accused indeed was right and he has a really good eye, because you can see here that I didn't see that the dates were different on the two versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So does that mean that this is not the correct document? It appears that this is not the correct document. The numbers not the same either, so could we find the correct document. We're grateful to the accused for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that it is the same document, but this may -- no, no. Everything is different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The names are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see that Katic, the name Katic is not mentioned here at all, and in the original you can see Katic. Well, if it hadn't been for the accused, I, for one, would not have noticed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we able to locate the correct document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted as a Defence exhibit in B/C/S; and once we've found the translation, then can we at least have it marked for identification and then admitted later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I at least conclude the examination of this witness now, because he doesn't need the translation and then we can get the translation later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go head.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be marked for identification as D199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, that is until we've received a translation. So now have I to -- I have to repeat my question. I will not go back to what happened at Pofalici and Mojmilo, so I will not be repeating this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But could you please now read the first paragraph, and then tell us whether this has anything to do -- whether these two things are in fact related?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of this preamble --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now we have the translation on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of the first preamble, and in view of what had happened at Pofalici and Mojmilo, there was an imminent threat of war. And a commission was established, not only for the Novo Sarajevo municipality. Such commissions were established in other municipalities. And as I stated three years ago, I was shown this piece of paper, but this commission never met with the members that are listed here throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to ask you -- you've explained to us that you had spent some time in the trenches, but I want to ask you whether you made any decisions that had to do with military activities.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, in the local authorities, and that goes for all municipalities, we could never make any decisions or exercise command over military structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we have this document admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as D199.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now, incidentally, I would like to show you Exhibit P496. Did the Prosecution show you this document several years ago, or whenever? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document. It was shown to me last year, again by the investigators in Sarajevo. So I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the first chapter in this document? You can first see the date. You can see who signed this order. So could you please tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please have this enlarged a little bit. I can say that I see here, "I have information that on 5th of November, 1994, a meeting took place between local leaders in Vogosca ... where a decision was made to block UNPROFOR, to confiscate heavy equipment under UNPROFOR control, and to shell civilians targets in Sarajevo with heavy weapons," lest I should now read everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read everything.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Bearing in mind that such a decision can have a long-term negative consequences for the Serbian people, and that these combat activities are being planned without my knowledge."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, please, could you read the first part of this document, before it says "I order."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I have information that on the 5th of November, 1994, a meeting took place between the -- of the local Serb leaders of Serbian Sarajevo in Vogosca, which was attended also by the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, where a decision was made it block UNPROFOR, to confiscate heavy equipment under UNPROFOR control, and to shell civilian targets in Sarajevo with heavy weapons, bearing in mind that such decisions can have long-term negative consequences for the Serbian people, and that these combat activities are being planned without my knowledge."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please stop.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me who signed this decision. Who is behind this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander, Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Sehovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander, Colonel-General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My first question to you is: As the president of a municipality, did you ever attend any such meeting? It says here that Mladic gained information, that some meetings were held between General Milosevic and the representatives of the civilian authorities. Did you ever attend any such meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, and that is what I stated to the prosecutors in Sarajevo. I say that I never attended such meetings as president of the municipality. According to what I saw here, the civilian authorities issue orders to a corps commander. I assert that I never attended such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that any civilian official ever took part or could take part in the bringing of such a decision?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single civilian, or rather, the representative of the civilian authorities at local level could take part in making such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard from anyone that General Milosevic at some gathering with the representatives of the civilian authorities decided to bomb Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I have not heard that, and I was not never present and never heard orders from General Milosevic that he would be hitting Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as you said a few moments ago, I have information, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask the witness whether, if such a meeting did take place between General Milosevic and the local Serb leaders, is it likely that he would have been one of those present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from this place now, I cannot claim that a meeting was held, when I was not there, when I was not present. However, on the basis of my knowledge, I think that such a meeting had not been held, because if all the presidents of the municipalities of the city of the Serb Sarajevo, it would have been logical for me to have been invited as well. However, I had not been invited and I had not attended such a meetings, even if such a meeting had been held per chance, but I don't think that such a meeting was ever held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, why then would General Mladic issue such an order? What is the background for this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do not understand, for this kind of document to come from General Mladic. On the other hand, I see that it is signed and sent on by Lieutenant-Colonel Milorad Sehovac. I think there were different stories going about, jealousy among officers, different calculations, so I do not believe that such an order and such an agreement could have been reached in the municipality of Vogosca, as stated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you suggest that General Mladic was misinformed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, well, as briefly as possible right now, so that we don't dwell on this document much longer. You, as a civilian representative of the people, if I can put it that way, when you met with General Milosevic, what were the dominant subjects of your talks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did meet with General Milosevic when he became commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The dominant subjects that we discussed were humanitarian aid, the protection of civilians at Grbavica, the protection of roads through Lukavica towards the Kasindol hospital, obtaining firewood. After large-scale fighting in the territory of Bjelasnica, Igman, further up north, the Nisic plateau, where the forces of the army of Republika Srpska were losing positions every day, if I can put it that way, and we had many fatalities among the soldiers, the General intervened through the civilian authorities, through me specifically, to have coffins obtained. When I talked about humanitarian aid, it was necessary to ensure as much food as possible, as well as fuel, and we did all of that through the civilian authorities. These were specifically my talks with General Milosevic and with other commanders of brigades that were within the corps, or rather, in charge of safeguarding the borders of the Serb municipality of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would that be the reason when he would go elsewhere, Ilidza, Rajlovac, Nedzarici, anywhere, when he would go to the representatives of the civilian authorities? Vogosca, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing what was discussed with me, I assume that the same thing was discussed with other presidents of municipalities, or rather, presidents of the Executive Boards of these mini-governments in different municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When the question was asked, I assumed that the witness would have personal knowledge of these meetings with other presidents of other municipality assemblies, but the witness has just stated that he has to make an assumption that is an extrapolation from the conversations he himself had with the accused. And so for reasons of lack of foundation, I'll object to the witness continuing with this answer, unless a proper foundation can be laid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. He can't really help us with that information, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll rephrase my question and, well, I will have to deal with the subject one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yours was the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. Was there an assembly of all the municipalities within the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, the city of the Serb Sarajevo was established consisting of six municipalities; namely, the Serb New Sarajevo; Pale; Stari Grad, the old city; the Serb municipality of the centre, Centar; Vogosca, Rajlovac; and Ilidza. And in 1994, the seat of this city was in the municipality of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you would meet, what did the meetings look like? Who would come to attend these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only presidents of Executive Boards of municipalities came to attend these meetings, as well as the presidents of the municipalities; that is to say, two persons respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these meetings, when you would all get together, what was the dominant topic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this was already 1994, what would happen was that the economy was not functioning. We would, say, look at an organisation to see how the economy could be stepped up, how people could find employment in these companies, how to organise the public utilities, the water works at city level, the power company at city level, then also sewage, garbage at city level. If not possible, then every municipality should set up its own mini-locations as garbage dumps. Because I can say that during 1994, from the point of view of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, there was less military activity. Sometimes gun-fire was heard from one side or the other, if I can put it that way, but there was a sort of a cease-fire. So these were the talks that dominated; that is to say, the functioning of joint companies and the economy as such, or rather, providing humanitarian aid and how to assist the representatives of the military in terms of food and fuel supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at the document again for a moment; and if we look at what it says here, when the General learned this - let's not go into it in any greater detail - what happened then? In the first paragraph. Let's not go any further. Let's just get this over with.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Without my explicit order or approval, I forbid undertaking any activities in connection with the blockade of UNPROFOR and confiscation ever heavy weaponry under its supervision without my explicit order and consent."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me what the time span was between the date when he learned of this and the date of the order itself? Can you see this in the document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is almost impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please. Look at the letterhead.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7th of November, and the meeting was held on the 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many days is that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you mentioned now this assembly where all the representatives of all the municipalities left -- or rather, took part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the permission of the Court, well, I did not put on my 65 ter list at all the map that we started using from the very outset, the UNPROFOR map that we showed practically all our witnesses. The document number is 289 -- no, 298. Could we have a look at this map, and can we use it in the future too? I have been using it practically every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that map, the UNPROFOR map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you show the place where the assembly of the entire area was, rather, where all the municipalities were together, that assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark that with a letter V.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now put a small dot where the building of the municipality was; that is to say, the municipality where you were president.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that practically at the separation line itself, between the two sides?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday, I said how far away the municipality was from the residence of Mr. Izetbegovic, 300 metres, so the municipality building was practically at the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark it with a letter G, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now draw a line of your route. How often did you attend these municipal assembly meetings every month?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, once a month, sometimes once in 20 days; but let me say, once a month we had meetings in Vogosca and sometimes in the municipality of Ilidza in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark Ilidza --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: -- with a letter I.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, can you please draw the line of the route that you had to take in order to get to these meetings concerning the problems that were at hand; and can you also describe, while you're drawing this line, what kind of problems you encountered?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first have to say that while I was president of the municipality, I didn't have either a driver or a personal escort. I went on my own, and I drove the car myself. I would set from Grbavica down the road towards Trebevic, exit Vraca, and then via Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, can you stop for a second?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This line, what does it represent, approximately? What is the location?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the location when you exit at Vraca, a to Trebevic via Miljevici and Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, please. What is the size of the area at Zlatiste from which perhaps one could see part of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road at Zlatiste, the passage leading to Osmice from which one can see Sarajevo, is about 150 metres long. The rest of the road goes through a forest and via Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please use another pen, another colour. While you were -- while you were a fighter, can you show and indicate the line where you were as a fighter. So next to this blue line, can you indicate the area where you were as a fighter?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now show us where Debelo Brdo is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who held the dominant elevation at Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war, from 1992 until the end of the conflict, the Debelo Brdo elevation was held by the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and I can say that while I was a soldier in 1992, from the positions near our houses, we always had Debelo Brdo in front of us, and we couldn't see Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the positions that you held, how far were they from Zlatiste?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The positions where I was to the peak of Zlatiste, the distance was about 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, from your positions, could you see at all -- I mean, I'm not going to lead you. What were you able to see? Can you explain that to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the positions where I was in 1992, I could see parts of Grbavica, or virtually the whole of Grbavica, and perhaps a small part of Kovacici. As far as the city was concerned, I could only see Velesici and Pofalici on the other side, and that is much further from the river Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark Debelo Brdo on the map with a letter D.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And there we must stop, Mr. Tapuskovic. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have a small technical problem relating to the markings which the witness made on the map. We have lost them, so I'm going to ask the witness to remark the map so we can have it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the floor, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, you have to mark again the place where Novo Sarajevo municipality was, just like you did last time, with a dot.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And put a letter G?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have to mark again Vogosca with a circle that you put before and put -- yes. Thank you. And the place where Ilidza is and put a letter I.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could now continue your movement on the map, after Zlatiste, what was the first place that you came across?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I left Zlatiste, the road leads on to Trebevic. I would come to Osmice where the separation line was at about 40, 50 metres. That was the so-called Andja's house, as everybody used to call it. On this section, and due to the geographical terrain, the vehicle have to slow down, and this poses a great danger to traffic at this particular spot. If we move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was around the road on this location?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the lower side is a wood and rocks immediately after you leave Zlatiste. There were rocks on both sides of the road, like a sort of a canyon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How big is the forest there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as you pass through these rocks on the other side, the wood is on both sides of the road in the direction of Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please now continue drawing the line and stop at the point where the forest ended. How big is this distance? Please continue drawing the line.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a fork on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. While you are passing through the wood, do you have any view from that point of the inner-city of Sarajevo? Could you see Grbavica, Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the road which I used to take, the forest blocked the view. These are big evergreen trees, and one cannot see parts of Sarajevo, including Bascarsija. These are very tall trees in this for rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So if you proceed further on, and keep drawing the line, which direction would you take?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a detour from the separation line towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then from Pale, how can you go back to this map again?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Returning from Pale, I would set off towards --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Draw it. Draw it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sumbolovac; that is to say, Hresa and Vucja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please keep drawing the line.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And here --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please stop for a moment. Now, while you were going down this road, did you encounter any problems?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I arrived with my vehicle to Hresa --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mark it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Put a letter H. And then when you proceeded, what happened on the road?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it is shown on the map, there are the lines here, and they're so close. One had to pass by Spicasta Stijena where, if I drove a car, I could only hear shots because that was a macadam and you couldn't drive fast. At one point, I would be in a position that I didn't know who was shooting and from where. The only important thing is to pass that section without being shot or without experiencing something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So in what direction did you then proceed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would go --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark -- please put an S. No, no, no, no. Spicasta Stijena.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Where you put the letter S, is that Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not where the letter S is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, put an S.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to put an S where Spicasta Stijena is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, in geographical terms, what is Spicasta Stijena? Geographically speaking, was that --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Geographically speaking, that was one of the higher elevations in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And it was part of which hill?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I used to pass there once in a month or once in 20 days, I think that it is part of Grdonj, or rather, these --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, where did you go next, and what happened in the subsequent areas or sections of the road?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to draw the road, and then I'm going to describe it for you. Once I passed Grdonj and Spicasta Stijena, I would go down through Mrkovici village and reach Radava.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please put a letter R for Radava.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was something happening there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the separation lines were close to each -- one another also, so that both Radava, which belonged to the centre municipality, and the road and this area could have been shot at or fired at from the Grdonj hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite. So while you were passing down these roads, were you able at all to see Sarajevo from these points, any part of Sarajevo, and where could it stop, if you can show us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from these areas that I just indicated where you pass, through here, it is impossible to see Sarajevo from any part until you move closer to the village of Poljane, further away from Radava.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is where it is, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what can you see from that point?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Poljane, you can see parts of Kosovo, Bare, in Sarajevo, that area, that is not as densely inhabited as the rest of Sarajevo, but parts of Bare, Kosovo, the Kosovo hill, and so on. And you can also see Hum and Kobilja Glava at Hum, and other places such as that, from this area if you look in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I'm asking. From Hum and from Zuc, what is your position in relation to Hum and Zuc?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am in a subordinate position because from Hum, Zuc, and Kobilja Glava, you can actually target those areas here at Poljane.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, as you move on to Vogosca, where is this line that you just drew, and the red line? But first draw the line to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what is the position of these two lines, the red and the blue line?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are more or less the separation lines where the road goes through those uninhabited, almost completely uninhabited areas entering the Pretis factory, going through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm asking you is: Those lines, in relation to the geographic positions of these areas, who is now in more favourable position if you look at those two lines, the red line, the blue line, and even the yellow line? Who has the dominating position over those areas?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the opposite side, here, there is the Hum hill; and from the positions there, this line can be targeted and is under threat from those positions. I think that -- that Hum is dominant; it's dominating these areas here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now please quickly draw there line all the way down to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure. This is how we went, more or less. This is where we actually diverge. I can say, since I didn't say that before, this road, the entire road, from the old town municipality, Hresa all the way up to Vogosca, this is a macadam road. You could not do more than 20 or 30 kilometres per hour. Our journalists sometimes referred to this road as the Road of Sun. I often used to say that for the inhabitants of Ilidza, Vogosca, and Rajlovac, this was the Road of Salvation. Because as the road was being made, and I know something about that, more than 20 per cent -- the slope is -- the gradient can more than 20 per cent. It was impossible to move there in winter, in particular, if the road was targeted, if there was fire, and the road traffic would be blocked for hours, not even ambulances could pass. If there was some seriously wounded or sick people, they could not be transported to Pale. As regards the road to Rajlovac, the Ilidza municipality, in other words, this entire road from Vogosca to Rajlovac was in a very precarious position because of the BH army positions. Because particularly near Rajlovac there were those dominating hills above Zobrezje, Sokolje, and other slopes leading to Rajlovac, where the inhabitants of Rajlovac were on the low ground and were daily exposed to fire from those areas that dominated this area. And there where the road diverged from Rajlovac and from the separation lines, this was a little bit safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the Vogosca-Ilidza road?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the road from Vogosca to Rajlovac, how danger it was; and then, and only when you pass the Rajlovac, there was a section in the direction of Ilidza that was a little bit safer because it diverged from the separation lines, from the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the Road of Salvation. What happened on that route, if the prevailing circumstances were as you just described them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if a vehicle passing through would be hit, and if there were in the casualties, some civilians or whoever was in the car, they were wounded, going from Ilidza, Vogosca, Rajlovac to Pale, then traffic would be blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you already said that. Could you please tell me, all those lines that you just described for us, were there any consequences for the human lives, both civilians and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for sure, because I would come across some vehicles that would be hit. They would be giving a lift to a civilian or soldier who had been wounded; and as I already described, this is quite a long route, maybe 50 kilometres, and there some critical points at several places, very exposed to fire from BH army, and, quite naturally, both soldiers and civilians alike would be -- there would be civilian and military casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me, why didn't you go straight to Grbavica when you got there from Ilidza using some other route. Was there any other route to Grbavica from Ilidza except this one?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until June 1992, members of the Republika Srpska army and civilians used the airport as a route between Ilidza and the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo; and then in June 1992, the airport came under -- under UNPROFOR control, and UNPROFOR had control over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And at the time of Dragomir Milosevic, were there any additional circumstances that made it easier for the people in Sarajevo to live, in relation to what you just said about the airport? I don't want to lead you on this.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was there underneath -- what was there at the airport? Could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, underneath the airport, a tunnel had been dug. It was used by the BH army to move from Sarajevo to other areas, other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were controlled by the Bosnia-Herzegovina army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But, first, answer to this question: How long did it take you to get from your assembly, if the session was in Ilidza, to get back home? How long did it take you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I headed out from Grbavica, and if the meeting was at Ilidza, it would take me about five or six hours because it's about 100 kilometres. When I had to travel from Grbavica to Ilidza via Pale, and if the meeting was scheduled for 10.00, I would start at 5.00 a.m., and I would come back at 10.00 p.m. That's when I would come home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, in winter, we know what Sarajevo is. Everybody knows what Sarajevo is. What was it like in winter?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in winter time, it was much, much tougher. First of all, this road that had been made during the war did not comply with any standards for macadam roads that could actually meet the demands of this kind of traffic; and then in the fall, there would be mud, and then in winter, if you didn't have good tires, if you didn't have snow chains, you couldn't even pass in many areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. How long did it take for civilians or soldiers from those areas that were in the area of responsibility of the BH army to get to Igman, for instance, or Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think if you used the tunnel and the road through Dobrinja from Sarajevo to the airport, I think -- I never took the route through the tunnel, not evenly after the war. I don't think it would take you more than two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If he has never taken the route through the tunnel, then I don't think he can of an opinion as to how long it takes to transit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As to how long it takes to transit it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: He was describing a route, and he said in his answer says, "I never took the route through the tunnel, not even after the war," and then proceeded to offer an opinion as to the duration, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he might have been told by somebody who had transited the tunnel. What would be the basis for the information that you are giving, as to the length of time that it would take to go through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, based on my knowledge of the streets of Sarajevo now and before the war, you could get to the tunnel from any part in half an hour. And no matter what conditions there were in the tunnel, and on the basis of what I know about the length of the tunnel, it would not take you more than an hour to pass through the tunnel; so that's an hour and a half, and then half an hour to get to Hrasnica. So these are the arguments that I use; and in my current post, the chief of traffic department, I can confirm that and I can actually state this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in order for us to include this last piece of information on this map, could you please draw the line from the part of Dobrinja that was under the control of the BH army in the direction of the tunnel, and then on to the edge of this map. Could you please draw this line. Your Honours -- in fact, Witness, could you please mark it with letter A.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But could you please draw the line out. This is Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you. So could this document please be given a number as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as D200.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, or maybe you can't, how many -- what was the distance in kilometres from Grbavica to Ilidza where you would finally reach your destination and then on the way back at the time of the events?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell that you Grbavica to Pale is 30 kilometres across the Trebevic; and from Pale to Ilidza, if you use this road, it's about 60 kilometres. So 90 to 100 kilometres, that's the distance between Grbavica and Ilidza, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know -- there was a hospital in Ilidza. What was it called?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Zica hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when it became operational?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was not in 1992. I think that it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to the wounded people, civilians or fighters, at the time -- at that time, 1992/1993? What happened to these people? Where did they have to go in order to get to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, there was no hospital in Ilidza. The wounded persons, regardless of whether they were civilians or soldiers, had to be taken to the Pale municipality where there was a hospital at Pale, and I also said what difficulties were involved. From Ilidza, a vehicle transporting the wounded person would take a minimum of three or four hours, even if the traffic was not blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, was the Zica hospital equipped for the most complex intraventions that had to be performed during the time of conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a doctor, and I assume that I will give only a partial answer to your question. Not a single hospital in Serb Sarajevo or in Kasindol or in Pale, and that probably includes Zica as well, did not have all the necessary instruments or equipment required of a modern hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, what had to be done with the seriously wounded, the seriously ill?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wounded who were hospitalised in these hospitals then had to be transferred to hospitals in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to Belgrade, and this was done by helicopter if approved by UNPROFOR, or by some other rapid means of transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If it was not approved, where did they have to go, which way, I mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road that I drew, to get to the Pale hospital. There was no other way to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am really mindful of the time because I know this is part of the Defence time. However, I have to keep the witness a bit longer. I will try to keep things as short as possible, but I know that I am within the limits of Defence time. I will do my best to cut things short, but I do ask you kindly to give me a bit more time to complete my questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tapuskovic, five hours had been allocated, I think, based on your estimate for the totality of this witness's evidence, and you have already used up about three hours and 20 minutes, which would leave the Prosecutor with two hours and -- no, less than two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what can we do? Let it even be at our own expense, but I'm compelled to do this. Your Honour, for example, Mr. Docherty -- let me explain this, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much longer will you take?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll hurry up. I really will. I'm not aware of this. Well, you see, I got this document which was wrong, and it is only now that I see this. The document is 03187 and it was wrongly submitted to me, and I don't know even know what this document is. I still don't have it in my hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. It means that we will not even be able to start the other witness who was scheduled to testify today, but, proceed. And after this witness, I'm going to be much, much more strict with the times of both parties. But I have always believed that counsel should have some leave, some freedom, in examination-in-chief. It's his case, after all. So proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, can you tell me what the main problems were that you had in your work in Grbavica, you as president of the municipality? Please try to focus on the most important things, and particularly on the period for which General Dragomir Milosevic was indicted.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how I'm going to start: In the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, the population was about 25.000. Throughout the war, in Grbavica, there were about 1.500 non-Serbs. The duty of the civilian authorities was to see how humanitarian aid would be distributed so that all the citizens would be satisfied. I ordered the secretary of the Red Cross of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo straight away to check out exactly how the aid was being distributed. I talked about this yesterday, what the situation was like in 1992, and we agreed that all the inhabitants of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo should receive humanitarian aid equally, irrespective of ethnicity. I even suggested that in buildings, Muslims or Croats should be commissioners in charge of the distribution of this humanitarian aid. I had yet another obligation; namely, that all citizens who were entitled to a pension had to receive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Judge Harhoff wanted to ask you something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I just wanted to clarify who was responsible for the distribution of humanitarian aid? Was that the ICRC or was it the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the International Red Cross brought in certain quantities of humanitarian aid to the area of Grbavica; and then on the basis of a list made by the secretary of the Red Cross, this list consisted of inhabitants of Grbavica and then exact quantities of food were allocated, so that all of the citizens of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo would receive the same amount of food; that is to say, that we received food from international institutions, but the secretary of the Red Cross of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo distributed it on the basis of lists of inhabitants. That is how the food was distributed. The members of the International Red Cross never distributed the food themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So who was responsible for the unequal distribution of humanitarian aid, which you referred to just a while ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was in 1992, when the assemblymen, because the authorities did not function properly in 1992, asked for a change of all the civilian authority in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. They were held responsible because they did not distribute food equally, if you understand me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, after this question from my colleague, I have a follow-up question. What was the place of the High Commissioner for Refugees, what was his role in relation to the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The High Commissioner to the Refugees was not represented in your municipality; is that it? Were there any refugees or displaced people in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were displaced persons from other areas, other parts of the town of Sarajevo. I don't know who was the High Commissioner for Refugees and Displaced Persons, but probably they visited the office of the Red Cross from time to time and checked to see what the distribution was like. I really did not have any meetings with the representatives of -- I mean, the representatives who were in charge of refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, what was the situation like in your time, as regards humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that at the time, while I was president, everything functioned properly as far as the distribution of humanitarian aid was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But a few moments ago, before Judge Harhoff put his question, you talked about pensions and what the situation was like in that respect. I would like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Its 65 ter number is 03180; it's a Prosecution document. There's a translation, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the date first, look at who issued this document, and just have a look at the heading, to see what it pertains to. Do you see the date? What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 11th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is stated in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior, Security Services Centre, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is the heading?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Record."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what comes then? What is this big part all about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The March Barricade."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It says, "Record," and what does it say after the big paragraph, underneath "Record"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is this text? Is this a statement, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, what is this? Can you see what is stated in big letters, the biggest letters after it stays "Record"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please pay attention to the text. You mentioned pensions a while ago, and now look at the middle of the text. Please look at the middle of the text, and now look at this word. It says, "Familiar." Could you read that part of the text? Read it out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
