utterances.text: From the middle of the text?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the word "poznato."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I know that the Muslim pensioners did not receive their pensions from the beginning of the war till about a month ago when a certain Katic, for whom it was being said around Grbavica that he was a good man, became the president of the so-called Serb municipality of Novo Sarajevo. That is when all the pensions were paid out retroactively, although they were not more than symbolic amounts. This move of paying out the pensions was commented upon among the Muslim residents, who remained in Grbavica, as a way of establishing the exact numbers of the Muslims left in Grbavica." I have to say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Slowly, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that all that time the Croat pensioners were receiving their pensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please go on now.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I have not heard that any of my neighbours were killed or abused in any way by the members of the aggressor's army."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now look at name, name of the citizen, the lady who made this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Citizen Muvedeta Tanovic; maiden name, Arslanagic. You want me to read all of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D201, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain just very briefly what it was like with regard to other matters that have to do with life in a certain environment. I don't want to be leading at all.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main thing that we bore in mind and that we dealt with in the municipality, especially at Grbavica, was the functioning of public utilities, whether there was electricity, water, and gas. I have to tell you that I had a very good cooperation with the members of G5 of the French Battalion who helped our companies in eliminating waste products to the dumps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please. Can we talk about the basics, the essentials. What was the situation like in your area, and what was it like in other areas?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as gas supplies were concerned, I can say --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Water, too; everything else as well.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. First, I will talk about gas and then water and then electricity. First of all, there no problems with gas. Throughout the conflict, there was gas in Sarajevo at Grbavica and elsewhere; and if there would be a leak somewhere in the pipes, then there would be a meeting between the representatives of companies on -- from both sides. So repairmen went out from both sides, and then they would repair what had to be repaired. As far as water was concerned, citizens stood in lines, like elsewhere in Sarajevo, in buildings that had more than three or four storeys. There wasn't any water there. And as far as electricity was concerned, also together with UNPROFOR, they dealt with the repairs, repairmen from both sides together with UNPROFOR, so that no one would get hurt during the intervention. It is only natural that when there is gun-fire, there is conflict, some transmission line would get damaged, but then there would be joint interventions in order to repair this. As things were in Sarajevo, they were in Grbavica, too. Proof of that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. What are you trying to say by it was the same in Sarajevo as in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning water, the citizens of Grbavica also stood in queues in order to pour water in their jerrycans and other vessels. I watched on TV that the same situation prevailed in other parts of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: If there is no water in Grbavica -- no, excuse me. If there was no water somewhere in the area of responsibility of the BH army, what was the situation in your area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only with local water supplies, like in Miljevici and Petrovici, water was available; but in Grbavica, there was not enough water as was the case in other parts of Sarajevo. The situation was totally identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me now - you already talked something about it - your contacts with military authorities, with whom did you meet most often from the military authorities, and can you please give me a quick answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I most often met with the commander of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade because it was their area of responsibility in Novo Sarajevo municipality, and we exclusively discussed the issues of ensuring the best food supplies for the army, how to provide firewood for the soldiers who were killed because the winter was coming, and how to improve the quality of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you communicate with liaison officers; and if you did, how did that look like?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I most often communicated with UNPROFOR liaison officers, the two officers in the corps command, if I needed any assistance from UNPROFOR. And we had a very good cooperation, as I said, with representatives of the GP French Battalion, with Medecins Sans Frontieres, and many others who were bringing aid, and we maintained all these contacts through the UNPROFOR liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You already explained how you had contacts with General Milosevic, but did he come to Grbavica; and if he came, what did you discuss with him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milosevic used to come to Grbavica when he wanted to inspect the position. He would always, as a rule, drop by my office where I was sitting as the president. We would have coffee, and we would, of course, talk about the situation on the lines and what was most needed for the army in terms of clothes, uniforms, oil, food, and other things. I said earlier that the General took due care about how people living in Grbavica could move freely and safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court what these photographs depict? I'm going to show to you two documents and each of them contains four photographs. We managed to obtain them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's document DD00-3335, page 21. No. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. What is this? Does this correspond to what you were just talking about? What does this represent?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first photograph, in the left-hand corner, you can see passages constructed and they were used by citizens, civilians, and soldiers, and these passages provided protection from gun-fire. You can see canvass sheets on the other photograph -- on the photograph next to it and blankets, which also provided passage for the people down the street. They couldn't physically protect people from gunshots, but they provided visual protection of the -- for the inhabitants of Grbavica. All these photographs are more or less identical. I explained that the area of Grbavica, and you probably could see, it's in the media, was a town with so many bricks, blankets, pipes of large diameter, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that situation approximately the same before this period?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we started putting these up in the 1994, in order to provide the protection for the people passing by, the protection for civilian, and automatically the soldiers on their way to their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this admitted as a Defence exhibit, these photographs, because it's a part of a larger document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we assume that you only want the pages admitted, the pages on the screen, because it's a huge document, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as D202.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us just take a look at another photograph, and can you tell me does that correspond to what you just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-3335, page 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me whether this is consistent with what you have just described.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's completely identical, only it depicts different positions; other parts of Grbavica, that is to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also have this document admitted as a Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, this can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like now to move to something that relates to military developments in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the 1st Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at one point a decision was taken with regard to heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. On the 5th of February, 1994, the Markale incident took place; immediately thereafter, a contingent of the Russian Battalion came to the former school of MUP in Vraca. And I think that in April or May, a decision was taken to relocate heavy weaponry from the Sarajevo area somewhere 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo. I remember that, and I think that it was done. Actually, I don't think; I know, and I assert that this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Did you go to the field as a representative of Sarajevo municipality; and if you did, what was the reason for your going?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, and one of the reasons was this incident. I wanted to see whether the weapons were removed. I went, together with representatives of UNPROFOR, to the village of Petrovici and Tvrdemici. This is all deep into the territory of Novo Sarajevo municipality where heavy weapons, tanks, mortars, 120-millimetre, and Howitzers were moved and covered with nets, and next to these weapons were members of the army of Republika Srpska and members of UNPROFOR, and they were guarding these weapons. I'm talking about the area of Novo Sarajevo municipality, but I also heard that in other areas the weapons were moved as well to some 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know when General Milosevic, approximately, became commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? At least, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was sometime in mid-August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me very briefly, because you did the job that you did, what did you know about the events involving combat activities between August and the end of 1994? What did you know about what was happening, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at Novo Sarajevo municipality, what can I say? In the area of Grbavica, or rather, in a broad area, including Lukavica, there were no significant combat activities. There was intermittent fire from both sides, and that would be approximately fire from infantry weapons. When I was in my office, I wasn't able to hear anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But did you know about events elsewhere, and how was that happening in general terms?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew about major conflicts in the area of Bjelasnica and in the area of Nisici plateau. I knew about that because many of my neighbours and other residents, including my brother, were often in those areas. I can say that those were very difficult combat periods and moments for the army of Republika Srpska. Many soldiers were killed or wounded. In some earlier statements, I said that I had talks with the general about the provision of coffins.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me very briefly something about the events in the period between the end of 1994 and May? Do you know -- well, let me not push this further.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the winter of 1994 and 1995, the winter was very harsh. There was a lot of snow, which means that there were no major combat activities in Grbavica. It was almost a truce, and I think it is very important to underline that open air market was functional. There were some incidents, and one of the most important incidents, at least in the eyes of us as civilian authorities, as well as for the residents, took place on the 11th of March, 1995, when two young girls were killed. They were about 10 years of age. They were playing in the park at Soping and were killed there from rifle fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you about this particular incident. But before that, I will show you document, 65 ter 03175. That's a Prosecution document. Let us look at it first and everywhere, and let us just look at the few last paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The document is 03178.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what is this, what is the date, and could you please tell us what kind of a document is it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a record of a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see whose statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out the name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Elvedin Bajrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please look at the last page of this document. It's a fairly long document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look. There are some parts that are underlined here. They were not underlined by the Defence, but could you please read what it says here, where it starts with "I learned from Amir Tahirovic." Could you read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I learned from Amir Tahirovic, a member of the work platoon, that members of the SPF had killed a person called Zlatko in retaliation in for the killing of two girls in Grbavica PZT. My neighbour, Selma, who lives at Zagrebacka Number 77, told me that the soldiers of the so-called Republika Srpska had killed Behko Ganic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you were the president of the municipality. This woman here says that had heard about that from someone. Did you hear about anything like that? Do you know anything about what is written here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear about this, and I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And since you were the president of the municipality, would it be possible for two murders to occur without you being aware of them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be impossible because, as the president, I had a briefing every morning with MUP chief in eastern Novo Sarajevo municipality, and he would have reported this to me. I don't know anything about this case, and I was not informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the previous page, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can move back, one page back. So this is the previous paragraph. I think that in English, it's fine. Okay. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read what this women says in her statement, the last paragraph on this page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 26th of April, 1995, we received an invitation which said that we should report to Sojic and fill out requests, which we did. We prepared two suitcases and two bags of clothes and crossed into the city on the 27th of April, 1995, taking up temporary residence at our Uncle Osman's place."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did this thing that this woman stated in her statement happen to other people, too, that they were allowed to go wherever they pleased?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This functioned, and people crossed the Brotherhood and Unity bridge from one side to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have this document admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D204, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me now, so this bridge was made and it is possible to cross it, under whose control was it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was primarily under UNPROFOR control. As we say, they were the chief Pope.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, if somebody wanted to cross to some other place at Grbavica, what would happen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if anybody attempted to cross at any other place, that person would be shot at and could be killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which side would fire at such a person?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the BH army side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serb side of open fire at civilian who is attempted to do something like that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like Defence Exhibit DD00-3211 to be shown to the witness. I had only one short portion of this document translated by the translator that I hired, and I would like the witness, once this document is up on the screen, to explain what it says in the heading and the underlined portions of it. And the Defence did not underline this. This was the original of the document, in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So could you please look up. It's not typed out. It's actually -- it is handwritten. Could you please see who actually issued this document, and what is it, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the command of 101st Brigade, 7th of April, 1995, daily combat report."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read this part in the middle that is underlined. Please make an effort, you have to read it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Last night at around 1930 hours, our fighters at Loris, mortally wounded an elderly person, a woman, who wanted to cross to the other side. She was pulled out to our side with UNPROFOR assistance. The identity of this person is not known."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We didn't have," something or other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the last part that is also underlined, "UNPROFOR activities"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR activities, apart from the activities related to the pulling out of the dead -- the person who was killed in the Loris area, there were no other activities."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So does this document clearly show what happened to this woman in the end?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the poor woman tried to cross not using the bridge from Sarajevo to the Serbian Novo Sarajevo side and she was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us what is Loris?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Loris is a building where the BH army soldiers were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have this document admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps that would be a convenient time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will take it normally at 20 past, but we can take it now. It's just two minutes away. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, I would like to us be as concise as possible. I have now come to the end. Regarding this incident with the two girls, what happened afterward. This was in March. So what happened until May? What was going on at the separation lines?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for the conflicts and things like that, in the period between March and May, there were no major clashes at Grbavica, just some sporadic rifle fire from the two sides, but no major clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what started to happen in May, and when did this reach this level of a larger scale conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May, the weapons from, in particular, the BH army side, became more intense, and we all felt it. We all heard it. We heard the fire. And in May, again, there were mostly rifles, no major shelling. But from day to day, we felt that the fire, more intense fire was opened on the positions of the Republika Srpska army, and I can say that this intensified even further in June with constant attacks on all the lines in the Grbavica territory and, in fact, in the broader region, which was in the area of responsibility of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade; in other words, on the entire side of the Novo Sarajevo municipality. Looking from the -- from my post, some larger calibre shells started hitting Grbavica. I was not able to determine whether this is cannon ammunition, shells, bombs. I couldn't determine the calibre, but it was constant, and this fire intensified day after day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when did it culminate in June?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I think it was on the 20th of June. This was the culmination of the conflict between the Bosnia-Herzegovina army and Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will show you two documents, and then I would like to ask you to look if they correspond to what was happening in the area that you were quite familiar with. So this is document DD00-3315.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document does not have a translation, just partially translated, but I would just like to ask the witness if he remembers on what axis were those combat activities most intense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What is it that you are showing to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've given up on this document. I'm not going to be using it, but I will show the witness another document. I wanted to show him a document that would indicate what was happening in those very first days when this offensive, the biggest offensive, was actually launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, could you tell us, what was happening in those days?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that a large-scale offensive was launched by the BH army on all positions in the area of responsibility of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade in the territory of Novo Sarajevo municipality. And, actually, the lines in Djukica Potok were broken through from the direction of Osrenska and the Mojmilo hill. Four our five of our soldiers were killed there and several were wounded. The second breakthrough was above Zlatiste at the famous Andja's house that I mentioned in my previous evidence, and four soldiers of the army of the Republika Srpska army were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: To cut a long story short, in this offensive and in all those conflicts, as far as you knew, did you have any information as to the number of civilians and soldiers who were killed at Grbavica, if you can give us this figure?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six to eight soldiers were killed in the 1st Sarajevo Brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreter is asking to you repeat the answer you just gave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Novo Sarajevo municipality area, in the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, because this was its area of responsibility, 608 soldiers were killed, around 460 of them were locals from the municipality; and around 650 civilians. I think that we are the municipality in Republika Srpska that suffered the worst casualties in relation to the overall number of people living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we were in a position to document that, are there appropriate documents for each and every one of these deaths?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for all people who lost their lives in Grbavica, or rather, the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, there are appropriate documents. And this refers to the period from 1992 until the end of the war, and it also pertains to all burials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you mention burials, could you tell me under what conditions people were buried, regardless of their faith or ethnicity, in the area of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What would be the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, during the day -- well, the I beg your pardon. At some points in time, it was impossible to have burials because there would be intensified fighting, and then people got killed again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Marginal, but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, could you ask the witness this, because we're dealing with figures. Here we have a figure of 608 soldiers who were killed and 650 civilians, but are we talking about soldiers of Serbian army or are they soldiers from all parties or armies?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, you heard -- you've heard the question of His Honour Judge Mindua. Can you answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 608 soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska from the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, and there are accurate figures on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are providing us with some figures, and this is compared to figures from the opposite side, from the ABiH, is it, or did you do this for another reason? I'm seeking to understand the relevance as well, the relevance of the figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already spoken about that several times, and I will say again this was the period of time when there was the largest number of casualties. These were combat activities, especially in Grbavica. But also in all other cases, at the time relevant to the indictment, there were responses to these combat activities when absolutely necessary. The only reason why there was occasional firing, especially in this case, was extreme military necessity; and then in such a clash there would be civilian victims, too, and soldiers were among the casualties as well, especially in this situation. I do not want to go into other things included in the indictment, such as deliberate targeting in order to kill someone. I should speak about that only when I analyse each and every individual case, and when we look at this period of time to see whether there were cases when civilians were the only target. That is one of the matters that the indictment deals with, in addition to the questions as to who was on the hills, who was firing from the hills. And in relation to that, have I one more question for the witness. The last document that have I to show him, I'd like him to tell me what it says to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Katic, would you please look at this document, DD00-3448. It was translated in part. Could you please explain what the letterhead says?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know how come there is no translation. I have the translation, but would it be possible for the witness just to read paragraph 2, because there is a combat report of the command of the 12th Division. I have the translation. I certainly do, but I don't know what happened now. Could at least be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him jest read paragraph 2. It's very short. No. You have to read it aloud so we can have the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "On all directions, reconnaissance and preparation of unit is taking place for the following combat days. 82-millimetre mortars were being fired from in order to carry out jamming and conduct works in the area of Osmice with six mortar shells. From Patmica [phoen] at Mojmilo, a Chetnik truck was hit at the road between Vraca and Lukavica, which remained on the road. After the truck was hit, the PAM crew continued firing at the truck."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that will do. Now I can put my question. At this point in time, in June, was this characteristic of what was going on? From Mojmilo, as it says here, where was most of the firing coming from? Actually, it was coming from Mojmilo, but they were firing at what?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is obvious from this report that from the hill of Mojmilo, it was the road that was targeted all the time between Vraca and Lukavica, Bijelo Polje, and that was the main road for civilians and soldiers, and ambulances, too, when they transported the seriously wounded, or women in labour, all the way to the hospital in Kasindol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be marked for identification as a Defence exhibit, but for identification, until it is translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tapuskovic, could you do us the favour when you bring documents to us that have not been translated to identify the provenance of the document. I assume this is an ABiH combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But it would be helpful if you would assist us so that we don't have to guess. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked for identification as D206.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I wanted to deal with this. What does the letterhead say? Who is the author of this document? What is this? What does this represent? What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Command of the 12th Division, strictly confidential, number 02/2-2-114, Sarajevo, the 20th of June, 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this paragraph that explains all of this, paragraph 2, what is its heading?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Information about our forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Can you tell me one more thing. What did this look like until the NATO strikes began?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's fine. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: July, August, what happened in June and July in particular, actually.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major combat activities continued at all positions, all positions of the army of Republika Srpska, that is, at Grbavica. Practically everything was on fire. You did not know where all the shells were coming from, where all the gunshots were coming from, and all the explosive devices, different ones. Quite simply, you couldn't get out into the street. At that time, I think it was in June, the Supreme Command declared a state of war in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, at this point, were you in these headquarters? What did you do about this when this was declared?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the state of war was declared, the assemblies of municipalities stopped operating; and in accordance with an order of the President of the state, war commissioners offices for municipalities were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You said, when you first started testifying, you talked about an imminent threat of war and then this staff was established. Was that the first declaration of a state of war, during the course of the entire war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the territory of Republika Srpska, never was a state of war declared; and now, in June, it was only declared in part and only in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber when the NATO airstrikes started?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. This was caused by an incident, if I can put it this way. Markale 2 happened on the 28th of August, 1995; and immediately on the 31st of August, the NATO bombing started and the rapid deployment force hit the Slavisa Vajner "Cica" and Slobodan Princip "Seljo" Barracks at Lukavica. Those were the names of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NATO airstrikes? No, none at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about strikes coming from someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What could be done at that point in time by the army of Republika Srpska, at all?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably they had to take all the weapons from 1994 that was stored on the basis of agreement and decision at certain sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know at all what was going on? Very soon weren't all these weapons actually handed over to NATO, or do you not know about this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. Were there any civilian casualties due to the NATO airstrikes?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I object to that on the ground of relevancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, explain the relevance, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the entire indictment, there is constant insistence, and I would like to point that out. There is constant insistence on the Serb forces being on the hills, and that their only target was - and that they did not have any other target as the indictment says - but to target civilians, and that was the only thing that the army of Republika Srpska did. If you think that this is not relative, whether these bombs under these conditions killed some civilians, too, then I really think that I don't have to explain anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the following: In these circumstances - let us disregard this question whether there were any civilian casualties - under these circumstances, do you know what at all what the army of Republika Srpska did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. Tapuskovic. Don't let me get mad. I have asked you to explain the relevance. I have to rule on it. It's absolutely out of order for to you direct a question to the witness before the Chamber has ruled. I'm going to consider the submission that you have made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand the submission that you have made to be the following: The Prosecution's case is that the army of the Republika Srpska targeted civilians, but you're saying civilians might also have been killed by NATO airstrikes. In that regard, and for that reason, the Chamber considers the question to be relevant, but you might want to direct the witness to an identification of the civilians who might have been killed by NATO airstrikes, so as to relate those incidents to the indictment, more particularly to the indictment. Do you understand the ruling that I have made?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honours, very much so. I'm not trying to find excuses for me. You have given me a valid -- valid reasons, but one cannot immediately respond to everything. My idea was that under such circumstances, collateral damage was unavoidable caused by any kind of bombs. This was my idea in that context. It wasn't my intention to claim that any fighting was directed purposefully; but that under such circumstances in a clash that could not have been avoided, resulted in collateral damage, including the one that we were just discussing. However, your ruling, it seems to me, is in that spirit. I didn't claim anything else, apart from the fact that collateral damage, under such circumstances, was unavoidable and that the killing of civilians was unavoidable in any clash and that it can be justified. This is what I wanted to say, and this is the position of my team. What you said is also appropriate. I may ask the witness whether he has information about civilian deaths and whether they can be identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the area of Novo Sarajevo, during the bombing, the NATO bombing of the Slavisa Vajner "Cica" and Slobodan Princip "Seljo" barracks, not a single civilian was killed, or a soldier, for that matter, in Lukavica, as a result of the bombing. But I did hear that there were people who were killed in Vogosca and in the area of Jahorina. I only heard about that, and I don't know whether those were civilians or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With this I have concluded my examination. Your Honours, one procedural matter. During the examination-in-chief, I was informed by my learned friend, the Prosecutor, that a document was erroneously disclosed to us which is on their list of exhibits, and that it has to be replaced with another document. In principle, as you know, we have to raise an objection to this. First of all, I didn't have an opportunity to see this, although the accused, Dragomir Milosevic, is never mentioned there, but I don't think this is permissible for me to learn about the existence of a document in the course of examination-in-chief. And for that reason, I cannot examine the witness with regard to that document because I didn't have a chance to analyse it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, do you know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, and it is unfortunate. We released the usual spreadsheet of documents we are go to use in cross-examination when the witness began his direct examination, as -- as protocol requires. This morning I was double-checking those documents and I realised that one of the documents, Minutes of a Crisis Staff meeting were, indeed Minutes of a Crisis Staff meeting, but from the wrong date. I wanted those of a different date. I disclosed the ones of a different date to the Defence at the first break today, apologised for the mistake, asked them if they would object on the grounds of late disclosure, retaining all other possible objections such as relevance and so on, and they said that they indeed would. And I told them that at an appropriate point in the cross-examination, I might, nevertheless, seek to use the document, but would, of course, tell the Chamber what had happened and would tell the Chamber also that the Defence objected on the grounds of late notice. I can tell the Chamber that, in light of the hour, I will not be seeking to use this document today. So there will be the weekend. I also will not object if Mr. Tapuskovic, on Monday morning, wants to reopen his direct examination for the purposes of examining the witness with regard to that one document. I hope that that solves the problem, which was my fault, and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in all these matters, the essential question is one of proper notice and whether the other party is prejudiced by the lateness; and for the reasons that the Prosecutor has outlined, and if we were to follow the procedure he has suggested, there will no prejudice to Mr. Tapuskovic, to the accused. He will not reach the document today so that you will have, Mr. Tapuskovic, and the accused, the weekend to review it. So no question of prejudice will arise; and if you wish to examine on it, then you will be allowed, either by way of re-examination or by some other procedure. Please begin, Mr. Docherty. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand. I could try and handle this in some manner in order not to get back to this. Give me just a moment to consult with my colleague. I didn't understand what you said, but I do agree with what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think the better course for you really is not to attempt to deal with it now, but take the weekend and look at the document, and on Monday, you come back to us and say whether you wish to re-examine on it on whether you wish to reopen your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's it. It's all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Katic. I know that you have met with other members of the Prosecution staff, but you and I have not met before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I do have a number of questions for you. If any of my questions are not clear, I'd ask you to please ask me to clear it up, rather than guessing at what I might have meant and trying and answering. Would that be all right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You've testified about several different topics during your direct examination, and you mentioned at one point, you testified at one point, that from the 13th of March, 1993 forwards, your duties were exclusively civilian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you were in the army, in the -- serving as a soldier in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, what rank did you have?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a rank. I was a private.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you were, during the time of the indictment period, you were not involved in any way in the day-to-day running of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you, therefore, would not know what orders, if any, were given by the accused, General Milosevic, to snipers, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know. I couldn't know whether the General gave orders relating to the sniper. I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the same would hold true for artillery and mortar units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You did, at one point, get appointed as what is called a war deputy, did you not? And we saw a document concerning that during your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a war commissioner in Novo Sarajevo municipality. That was the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That was the title, and I believe that you said when you met with members of the Prosecutor's staff, back there 2004, that you never attended any meetings in your capacity as a war commissioner and, indeed, never really did anything as a war commissioner, nor were you ever asked to do anything as a war commissioner. Is that a fair summation, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I said that the appointed war commission for Novo Sarajevo municipality never met again in that composition. That's what I said in 2004 as well. That's what I told the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so even though the title is "war commissioner," the fact that you served as a war commissioner for a period of time, we should not read into that any particular military expertise on your part?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You did as a civilian leader, president of a municipal assembly, have meetings, however, with -- at which military officers were sometimes in attendance; did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the assembly session was convened, someone would describe the situation on behalf of the brigade, among the soldiers, in the brigade itself, and to tell us whether there were any problems in that domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And when you say that the assembly met, those are the meetings in Vogosca that you were testifying about an hour or so ago and describing your route all the way around the city. Are those the meetings that you are referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was referring to regular sessions of the municipal assembly of Novo Sarajevo, where only the military situation in the area of Grbavica was discussed, or rather, in Novo Sarajevo municipality. Those were regular monthly assembly meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate the clarification. And from time to time, in the course of performing your civilian duties, you did encounter General Dragomir Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: He came to Sarajevo or to Grbavica from time to time. I believe you said that in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2004?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he came. Mr. Milosevic used to come to Grbavica; But I think that in 2004, I wasn't asked about General Milosevic, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when General Milosevic would come to Grbavica, as far as you could tell, he was there to meet with commanders of subordinate units, brigade commanders and battalion commanders; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the general would come to Grbavica, he would meet the battalion commander whose area of responsibility covered Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so did it seem to you that General Milosevic was taking steps to keep himself informed fully of what was going on militarily in Grbavica, by meeting with battalion commanders on a regular or perhaps semi-regular basis?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wanted to know what the situation was on the lines, whether the strength and the disposition of soldiers was okay, what was the morale like among the soldiers, whether they lacked anything. So this was what the general and his subordinate officers talked about; and when he came to see me, we talked only about the problems of humanitarian nature, the protection of the population in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I know it's been a while, but about how often during 1994 and 1995 or how often when he was commander of the corps did General Milosevic come to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps once a month. Perhaps even less than that, if -- if you're referring to his meetings with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes. The meetings we've been talking about up until now, when the general would come and meet with his commanders and then would meet with you, are you saying that happened about once a month or maybe a little less?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the general would meet me, only me, without his subordinate officers, once a month or even less often than that. And I don't know how many times a month the general would meet his subordinate officers. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And also, from your time in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps - granted as a private soldier - you understood that the corps had radios and field telephones and other methods by which they could keep in -- by which units of the corps could keep in touch with each other and could keep in touch with headquarters at the barracks in Lukavica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the field telephones. They had those traps, and then there would be a wire you would stretch a wire, at least that was in that area where I served as a soldier, and then they were linked with the command of their unit. We did not have any communications of that sort with the Lukavica Barracks, so the line went only to those units, not to the Lukavica Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so your understanding was the field telephone line went to the next unit and then that went up to the and the next unit next, and eventually somebody is talking to Lukavica Barracks. It's not you, but somebody is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably that's how it was. In accordance with establishment, somebody had to be in communication with the Lukavica Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this that is what is known in an army as a chain of command, is that right, Mr. Katic, in which a senior commander gives order to a junior commander and so on and so on down the line, until it reaches the soldiers on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we see again please Exhibit P 496, the order from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Katic, you were asked some questions about this document on your direct examination, and I just have a few more. First of all, in the first line, that is the document itself and not addresses and so on, I'll reed it out in English. "I have an information that on 5 November 1994, a meeting took place between local Serb leaders of Serbian Sarajevo in Vogosca." Do you see the part that I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And Vogosca is the place that you described in your direct examination as the 90-kilometre drive on bad roads to get to where the leadership of all of Serb Sarajevo, and not just Grbavica, would meet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said from Grbavica to Ilidza, it's 90 kilometres, and it's maybe 15 or 20 kilometres less to Vogosca. So from Lukavica to Vogosca, it's about 70 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. But regardless of the distance, Vogosca is the place where the leadership of all of Serb Sarajevo met from time to time. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And just as with the meetings that you had in Grbavica, where military officers would attend from time to time as -- if their input was needed, so military officers would attend meetings in Vogosca, if it was relevant for them to be there, if there was something to be discussed that their input was needed on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the civilian authorities meet, then only the presidents of municipalities, presidents of the Executive Boards, and the appointed president or the mayor of the city of Serbian Sarajevo, and the president of the Executive Board of the city of Serbian Sarajevo would meet. So only the civilian structures, the civilian authority would meet. But if there is an assembly attended by the deputies from all of the municipalities in Serbian Sarajevo, then those sessions would be attended by representatives of the military authorities who would be invited to do so, so only to the sessions of the assembly of Serbian Sarajevo. Just as I said, when the municipal assembly of Novo Sarajevo would meet, then we would invite the commander of the area of responsibility, that included that municipality to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now I want to take a look at what General Mladic's order actually says, and I'm going to read under order number 1: "I forbid undertaking any activities in connection to the blockade of UNPROFOR and confiscation of heavy weaponry under its supervision without my explicit order and consent." Do you see where I have been reading?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that doesn't say that UNPROFOR is not to be blockaded, and it doesn't say that heavy weaponry is not to be confiscated. It just says it is not to be done unless Ratko Mladic says so. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KATIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'd be happy to. My question is about the meaning of subparagraph 1 under "Order," and I'll ask you just to read it yourself, and my question is: That doesn't really say that confiscating heavy weaponry is forbidden, and it doesn't really say that blockading UNPROFOR is forbidden. What it says it that it is not to be done unless General Ratko Mladic says it is to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this witness be asked to interpreter an order, to interpret an order that is quite explicit? Somebody else should be asked to do so, in particular, the person who actually drafted. But to ask this witness to speculate what the person who ordered it actually meant, this is not permissible. Only Mladic could answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I don't agree. It's simply a question of saying whether he agrees with the meaning of the words attributed to them by the Prosecutor. There's no speculation there. It may be a question of language, Mr. Docherty, and maybe it's difficult for the witness to understand the question that you have put.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The key word is, "I prohibit." In our language, that means that's the key -- that that Serbian word is the key word. That's the key word, in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see that that is the key word, but the Prosecutor is asking the witness whether he agrees that the prohibition is not an absolute one. It is simply that these things identified as being prohibited are not to be done without the order and consent of Ratko Mladic. Do you understand the question which was put to you by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand the question and the way the order is phrased. The best thing would be to have the words "I prohibit," anything to be done right at the beginning. In my opinion, this is a very convoluted way of putting things, so that I really couldn't answer this question that Mr. Prosecutor has asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether Mr. Mladic would be happy to hear your criticism of his language. Mr. Docherty, we are at the time now for the break, and I have an administrative decision to give. I give a decision as to how the Chamber will organise its work on Fridays. On Friday, the 15th of June, there will be no hearing; Friday, the 22nd of June, we will sit from 9.00 a.m. to 5.00 p.m.; Friday, 29th of June, no hearing; Monday, the 2nd of July, no hearing; Friday, the 6th of July, we'll sit from 9.00 to 1.45; Friday, 13th of July, from 9.00 to 5.00; Friday, the 20th of July, no hearing; and Friday, the 27th of July, no hearing. This order will be filed with the registrar today. We're adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 4th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
